propositions.text: The Appellant is a citizen of Pakistan and appeals the RPD's rejection of his refugee claim.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Pakistan. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant is a Pakistani citizen appealing the RPD's rejection of his refugee claim.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's decision that the Appellant is not a refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant worked in Greece 2011-2013, returned to Pakistan, started a business, and was extorted by Lashkar-e-Taiba members in 2013.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that after working in Greece from 2011 to 2013, he returned to Pakistan and started a small business. In August 2013 he was approached at his business by four men collecting donations for the group Lashkar-e-Taiba.

propositions.text: The Appellant paid extortion money after a week on a friend's advice, who also advised against going to police due to collusion.
propositions.quote: These men demanded ?XXXX XXXX XXXX, which the Appellant paid after one week on the advice of his friend. His friend also advised him not to go to the police because the police always protect these groups.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges he was extorted by Lashkar-e-Taiba in Pakistan and advised not to go to police due to collusion.

propositions.text: The Appellant tried to convince other store owners to resist extortion; was beaten and threatened with death in 2014.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was aware that other store owners in his town were victims of extortion and he tried to convince them slowly and gradually about standing up to the extortionists. In XXXX 2014 two men came to his store and told him that they knew what he was doing and beat him. They demanded a further donation of ?XXXX XXXX XXXX and gave him a deadline of three days to pay.

propositions.text: The Appellant was chased, escaped, and his home was attacked with threats to kill him.
propositions.quote: After a couple of days he was chased by some people but was able to escape and went to a friend's home before returning home. At home he was advised that the men had been there and fired at their walls and kicked the door. The men told his mother that they would kill the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges he was beaten, threatened, chased, and his home attacked by extortionists in 2014.

propositions.text: The Appellant moved to his aunt's house but was chased; then moved to Sialkot and left Pakistan in 2014, arriving in the US in 2015.
propositions.quote: The Appellant moved to his aunt's house in another town, but was chased by two men on the street. He was able to hide in a bakery, but was worried about this new situation. The Appellant moved to Sialkot and began to make arrangements to leave Pakistan. He left in XXXX 2014 and eventually arrived in the US on XXXX XXXX, 2015.

propositions.text: He claimed asylum in the US but could not get a work permit and later came to Canada in 2018.
propositions.quote: He made a claim for asylum in the US, but was unable to get a work permit. He eventually decided to leave the US and come to Canada in XXXX 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant fled Pakistan, sought asylum in the US without work permit, then came to Canada in 2018.

propositions.text: The RPD heard the Appellant's refugee claim on August 10, 2018 and rejected it on October 4, 2018 due to lack of state protection and credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's claim for refugee protection was heard on August 10, 2018. In a decision dated October 4, 2018 the RPD rejected his claim finding that the Appellant had not established that state protection was unavailable and that there were credibility concerns regarding omissions from his Basis of Claim (BOC).

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the Appellant's refugee claim in 2018 citing state protection availability and credibility issues.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in assessing state protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in assessing state protection.

propositions.text: The RPD found no evidence that state protection was unavailable; Appellant never sought police protection after six incidents.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the evidence in the record did not show that the Appellant was unable to receive operationally adequate state protection in Pakistan. The RPD noted that the Appellant never made any attempt to obtain protection after six incidents.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected Appellant's claim of police collusion and murder of other store owners as not mentioned in BOC and explanation not credible.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation that going to the police was never an option because the government colluded with the Lashkar-e-Taiba and other store owners who had gone to the police seeking protection had been murdered, as these murderers were not mentioned in his BOC narrative. The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation for this omission, which was that the BOC was only about his own experiences.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no evidence state protection was unavailable and rejected Appellant's police collusion claim due to BOC omissions.

propositions.text: The RPD found police report showed police registered and investigated a storeowner's murder, contradicting Appellant's claim that perpetrators are always unknown.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that despite the Appellant's testimony that terrorist perpetrators are always listed as unknown persons in police reports, the police report he did submit into evidence regarding a storeowner who had been murdered shows that it was the brother of the storeowner who reported the attacker as an unknown person and that the police registered the case and initiated an investigation.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found police did register and investigate a storeowner's murder, contradicting Appellant's claim.

propositions.text: The RPD found Appellant's explanations about omission of a storeowner's murder from BOC contradictory and not credible.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant's explanation about the omission of the murder of a storeowner in his town from his BOC was contradictory and not credible.

propositions.text: Appellant first said he heard about the murder after BOC submission, then changed to hearing about it before submission, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's first explanation was that his BOC had already been submitted when he heard about this incident. When it was pointed out to him that the incident preceded the submission of his BOC he then stated that he actually heard about the story in XXXX 2018.

propositions.text: The DVD about the storeowner's murder showed no link to Appellant and had little probative value.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the DVD provided by the Appellant about the storeowner's murder showed no link between the Appellant and the victim and gave it a little probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Appellant's explanations about omission of a murder from BOC contradictory and the DVD evidence weak.

propositions.text: The RPD noted affidavits stating Lashkar-e-Taiba sought Appellant at family home as late as 2018.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered the affidavits from family and friends to support the allegations and noted that the mother's affidavit stated that the Lashkar-e-Taiba was looking for him at the family home as late as XXXX 2018.

propositions.text: The RPD found it implausible Lashkar-e-Taiba would not know Appellant left Pakistan in 2014 yet continue searching family home repeatedly.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the Lashkar-e-Taiba had no continuing interest in the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found affidavits stating Lashkar-e-Taiba sought Appellant in 2018 but found it implausible they did not know he left Pakistan.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues police efficacy varies by district and Pakistan's police suffer severe deficiencies and poor human rights record.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the documentary evidence states that the efficacy of the police varies greatly by district ranging from reasonably good to effective and that Pakistan's police system suffers severe deficiencies in many areas including equipment, technology, personnel training and intelligence capability. He submits that Pakistan's police force is under resourced, poorly trained and has a poor human rights record.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues Pakistan's police are under-resourced, poorly trained, and have a poor human rights record.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues he did not seek police protection because police would collude with Lashkar-e-Taiba to extort money.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he did not go to the police for protection because the police would have ganged up with the Lashkar-e-Taiba to secure some of the extortion money and would not provide protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues police would collude with Lashkar-e-Taiba and not provide protection.

propositions.text: The RAD notes Lashkar-e-Taiba is an anti-Indian group supported by Pakistani military and intelligence, threatening opponents and Shiites.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the country condition documentary evidence indicates that the Lashkar-e-Talba is an anti-Indian group focused on the Kashmir dispute and that it operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence.1 It is noted in a BBC article that people who oppose pro-Pakistan groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad are "threatened, beaten up and arrested". According to Freedom House, the tension between pro-Pakistan groups and pro-independence groups has led to increased attacks against Shiites.2

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Lashkar-e-Taiba is an anti-Indian group supported by Pakistani military and intelligence, threatening opponents and Shiites.

propositions.text: The RAD notes Lashkar-e-Taiba's funding comes from Pakistan state, Gulf charities, and illicit activities, but not extortion of local businesses.
propositions.quote: The RAD has considered the documentary evidence regarding terrorist financing. It is noted in the Canadian document Terrorist Financing Assessment 2018 3 that the Lashkar-e-Taiba relies on diverse revenue streams and a significant portion of the group's financial and material support originates from the state of Pakistan, as well as charitable donations from the Gulf States, charities and expatriate communities and businessmen. It is also noted that the group systematically exploits its non-militant arm, Jamaat-ud-dawa, for its social welfare networks. The group also diverts revenues and tuition fees raised from its Islamic institutions, medical clinics and services. The group also relies heavily on informal international money transfers and cash couriers. The RAD notes that not included in its fundraising activities is extortion of local businesses.

propositions.text: Other groups extort local businesses, but Lashkar-e-Taiba does not appear to use extortion as fundraising.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Terrorist Financing Assessment 2018 document contains information about other organizations, such as the Haqqani Network, extorting and levying taxes on local, regional and international businesses and citizens in its area of control. However this does not appear to be a fundraising method used by the Lashkar-e-Taiba.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Lashkar-e-Taiba does not use extortion of local businesses as a fundraising method.

propositions.text: No documentary evidence shows Lashkar-e-Taiba extorts local businessmen; police report and news do not identify perpetrators of a murder.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that there is no country condition documentary evidence on the record showing that extortion of local businessmen is a fundraising method of the Lashkar-e-Taiba. Furthermore, the police report and news item relating to the murder of a local businessman4 does not indicate who the perpetrator was or the name of the organization the perpetrator belonged to.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleged other businessmen were targeted and killed by Lashkar-e-Taiba but provided no supporting documentation.
propositions.quote: Although the Appellant alleged that other businessmen in his area had been targeted and killed by the Lashkar-e-Taiba, he has provided no supporting documentation regarding these murderers.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no evidence Lashkar-e-Taiba extorts local businessmen; Appellant's allegations lack documentation.

propositions.text: The RAD accepts on balance of probabilities that Lashkar-e-Taiba members attempted to extort the Appellant but finds it a localized situation.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant has provided several affidavits which reflect the information contained in his BOC, that he was extorted by members of the Lashkar-e-Taiba. The RAD will accept on a balance of probabilities that members of this organizations did attempt to extort money from the Appellant based on these affidavits. However, the RAD finds that this is a localized situation as it is not part of the documented methods used by the Lashkar-e-Taiba to raise funds.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD accepts Lashkar-e-Taiba extorted the Appellant but finds it a localized incident, not a common fundraising method.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the affidavit of the murdered businessman's brother has limited value due to lack of supporting evidence and Appellant's omission in BOC.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the affidavit of the brother of the businessman who was killed5 has limited value as the information contained in this affidavit is not supported by the police report and news item noted earlier. Furthermore, the RAD notes that it is stated in the affidavit that the Appellant was a good friend of his brother who was killed in XXXX 2017. The RAD finds it suspect that the Appellant would not mention the death of a similarly-situated person who was a good friend in his BOC.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with RPD that Appellant's explanation for omission was unreasonable and little weight can be given to the affidavit.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that question 2 (a) asks whether persons in similar situations experienced such harm, mistreatment or threats and to indicate the dates, names and places, wherever possible. Given this direction, and the Appellant's close relationship with the murdered man, the RAD agrees with the RPD that the Appellant's explanation that he thought he just had to write about himself, was not reasonable. Furthermore, the Appellant was represented by counsel in the preparation of his BOC. The RAD finds that little weight can be assigned to the brother's affidavit given this omission from the BOC and the lack of information contained in the supporting documents regarding who were the perpetrators of the crime.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the affidavit of the murdered businessman's brother has limited value due to omissions and lack of evidence.

propositions.text: The RAD finds it reasonable the Appellant would not approach police due to Lashkar-e-Taiba's alleged support by Pakistani military and intelligence.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the documentary evidence does indicate that the Lashkar-e-Taiba operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence. The RAD finds, given this information, that it was reasonable that the Appellant would not approach the local police in his particular circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds it reasonable the Appellant avoided police due to Lashkar-e-Taiba's alleged support by Pakistani military and intelligence.

propositions.text: The RAD finds Appellant has not shown persecutors can find him anywhere in Pakistan and that he has a viable internal flight alternative.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that the individuals seeking him out have the ability or will to find him anywhere in Pakistan. ... The RAD therefore finds that the Appellant has a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) elsewhere in the country.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellant has not shown persecutors can find him anywhere and has a viable internal flight alternative.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's claim lacked credibility or plausibility and did not consider internal flight alternative.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant had not established that the core elements of the claim were credible or plausible and did not therefore consider the issue of internal flight alternative.

propositions.text: The RPD noted the Appellant said he would be tracked anywhere in Pakistan including Karachi, far from his home.
propositions.quote: the RPD did note in its decision that the Appellant had stated that he would be tracked anywhere in Pakistan including Karachi, which is over XXXX XXXX XXXX km away from his home.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's claim not credible and noted he said he could be tracked anywhere in Pakistan including Karachi, far from home.

propositions.text: The RAD requested and received submissions from the Appellant on internal flight alternative in Karachi or Lahore on March 25, 2019.
propositions.quote: The RAD requested submissions from the Appellant in regard to the issue of a proposed IFA in Karachi or Lahore, which were received by the RAD on March 25, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD requested and received the Appellant's submissions on internal flight alternative in Karachi or Lahore.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues no viable IFA in Pakistan due to fear of militant group targeting him anywhere.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he does not have a viable IFA anywhere in Pakistan, including Karachi or Lahore because of his fear of the militant group in Pakistan and his belief that this group could target him anywhere in the country.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits Lashkar-e-Taiba is based near Lahore with several thousand members, making Lahore not viable IFA geographically.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the documentary evidence regarding the Lashkar-e-Taiba states that the organization is based near Lahore and that there are several thousand members. He submits that Lahore cannot be a viable IFA due to geographical reasons

propositions.text: The Appellant submits Karachi is not viable IFA given the size of the militant group.
propositions.quote: and that Karachi is not a viable IFA given the size of the group.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues no viable IFA in Pakistan due to militant group fear, submits Lahore and Karachi are not viable IFAs.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues Lashkar-e-Taiba has ties to global militant Islamist groups and has assisted Al-Qaeda.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that Lashkar e Taiba has significant ties to global militant Islamist organizations and that it has assisted Al-Qaeda.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits Lashkar-e-Taiba allied with other militant groups against Indian military in Kashmir.
propositions.quote: He submits that Lashkar-e-Taiba has formed alliances with Harkatul-Mujhaideen (HM), Hizb-ul-Mujhaideen (HuM), Jaish-e-Muhammed (JeM) and Harkatul-Jihadi-lslami (Hull) against Indian military assets in India-controlled Kashmir.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues high likelihood of persecution by Lashkar-e-Taiba or allies due to ties with other militant groups.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that given the ties with other militant groups, there is a high likelihood that he would be persecuted by the Lashkar-e-Taiba or its allies.

propositions.text: Ordinary Pakistanis opposing Taliban or not following sharia law have been subjected to violence by these groups.
propositions.quote: Ordinary Pakistanis, students and those perceived to be opposing the Taliban and other groups, or are not following sharia law, have been subjected to violence by these groups.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence states authorities do not adequately protect vulnerable individuals and delay investigating perpetrators like Lashkar-e-Taiba.
propositions.quote: He argues that the documentary evidence states that the authorities do not adequately protect vulnerable individuals, and have refrained from promptly investigating perpetrators of activities including abduction for ransom by groups like the Haqqani Network and Lashkar-e-Taiba.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues Lashkar-e-Taiba's militant ties increase persecution risk and authorities inadequately protect vulnerable individuals.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Appellant has a viable IFA in Karachi based on country condition evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed the record and finds that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Karachi.

propositions.text: Country evidence states living in areas occupied by militant groups does not automatically create protection need; risk depends on profile and threat nature.
propositions.quote: the country condition documentary evidence states that simply living in an area occupied, either wholly or partly, by the Pakistani Taliban or other militant groups does not give rise to a protection need. In general the risks from the Pakistani Taliban or other militant groups will depend on the particular profile of the person, the nature of the threat and how far it would extend.

propositions.text: Primary targets of militant groups include political/tribal leaders, security forces, and minority religious groups.
propositions.quote: Primary targets include political and/or tribal leaders, security forces and minority religious groups.

propositions.text: Ordinary Pakistanis opposing Taliban or not following sharia law have also faced violence by militant groups.
propositions.quote: However, ordinary Pakistanis, including students and those perceived to be opposing the Taliban and other militant groups or not following sharia law, have also been subjected to violence by these groups.

propositions.text: Risk highest in areas with armed anti-government groups: Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, FATA, and Baluchistan.
propositions.quote: Those main areas are: Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (formerly known as North West Frontier Province); the semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) that have a strong Taliban presence; and Baluchistan, where separatists are seeking greater political autonomy and control over local mineral resources.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Karachi a viable IFA; risk depends on profile and threat, highest in certain regions, ordinary Pakistanis also face violence.

propositions.text: Threat to Appellant localized to Lashkar-e-Taiba members in home area; no evidence they found him elsewhere or after 2014.
propositions.quote: the RAD has found that the threat to the Appellant was localized to members of the Lashkar-e-Taiba in his home area of XXXX. Although these people allegedly discovered the Appellant in 2014 near his aunt's home approximately four hours distance away by car, there is no information in the record that they were able to discover his whereabouts at any other time, or that he had left Pakistan in 2014.

propositions.text: No evidence Lashkar-e-Taiba knew aunt's home or visited it to find Appellant after 2014.
propositions.quote: there is no evidence on the record that they knew where his aunt lived or that they visited her home at any time looking for him.

propositions.text: Appellant's family still lives in home area; no evidence of harm attempts to family to find Appellant.
propositions.quote: the Appellant's family has continued to live in XXXX and other than people coming to the family home asking about him, there is no evidence in the record that any attempts were made to harm family members in order to locate the Appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant was a small business owner, not a high profile opponent, who refused to pay extortion money.
propositions.quote: the Appellant was not a high profile opponent of the Lashkar-e-Taiba; rather he was a small business owner who did not want to pay extortion money.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence Lashkar-e-Taiba would aggressively seek Appellant nationwide using government ties, especially after 5 years abroad with no contact.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that there is insufficient information in the record to establish that members of this group would aggressively seek him out all over the country using its ties with the Pakistan government in order to locate him so that he could pay a bribe of ?XXXX, especially since the Appellant has been out of the country for five years and has had no contact with members of this group since he left Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds threat localized to Lashkar-e-Taiba in home area; no evidence they sought Appellant elsewhere or after he left Pakistan.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows Lashkar-e-Taiba fundraising does not include extortion of business owners, focusing on schools, remittances, drugs, and counterfeiting.
propositions.quote: The RAD has further considered the documentary evidence showing that the fundraising activities of the Lashkar-e-Taiba do not include extortion of business owners and are focused on raising funds through legitimate means through schools, international remittances and donations and through less legitimate means such as drug trafficking and counterfeiting currency.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes Lashkar-e-Taiba fundraising excludes extortion of business owners, focusing on other means.

propositions.text: Karachi, a large city with 25 million people, is a viable IFA for the Appellant.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that Karachi, which is a huge city with a population of approximately 25 million people, is a viable IFA for the Appellant.

propositions.text: Security operations in Karachi have reduced militant violence; some areas are relatively safe.
propositions.quote: It is noted in the documentary evidence that security operations in Karachi have significantly reduced the level of militant and sectarian violence in recent years and that there are areas of the city that are relatively safe.

propositions.text: Large urban centres like Karachi offer ethnically and religiously diverse populations and anonymity for those fleeing violence.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence indicates that large urban centres such as Karachi, Islamabad and Lahore tend to have ethnically and religiously diverse populations, and offer a level of anonymity for people seeking refuge from violence by non-state actors.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Karachi a viable IFA with reduced violence and diverse populations offering anonymity.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges Lashkar-e-Taiba connected to Pakistani government and intelligence agencies.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that Lashkar-e-Taiba is connected with the Pakistani government and police forces, and the country condition documentation indicate that it operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence.

propositions.text: Evidence does not show local Lashkar-e-Taiba used government resources to find Appellant in Sialkot or after he left Pakistan.
propositions.quote: However, as noted earlier, the evidence in the record does not indicate that the local members of the Lashkar-e-Taiba in Gujranwala who were extorting money from the Appellant availed themselves of the resources of the Pakistani military and intelligence service given that they did not locate the Appellant in Sialkot where he resided for over three months and were not aware that he had left the country.

propositions.text: Only evidence of continuing interest was Lashkar-e-Taiba agents asking about Appellant at family home.
propositions.quote: The only evidence of continuing interest in the Appellant by the agents of persecution was that they went to his family home in XXXX and asked about him.

propositions.text: On balance, Lashkar-e-Taiba would not seek Appellant in Karachi if he relocated there.
propositions.quote: Given this history, the RAD finds on a balance of probabilities that the Lashkar-e-Taiba would not seek out the Appellant in Karachi should he relocate to that city.

propositions.text: Government's limited resources limit law enforcement effectiveness.
propositions.quote: The RAD furthermore notes the documentary evidence which states that a lack of resources limited the government's ability to implement effective control and enforce the law.

propositions.text: It is not plausible government would use limited resources to search nationwide for a low-profile person to satisfy low-level militants.
propositions.quote: The RAD does not find it plausible in these circumstances that the government would use its limited resources to search all over Pakistan for a person who does not have a high profile, in order to satisfy low-level members of a banned terrorist organization who wish to extort money from a business owner.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no evidence Lashkar-e-Taiba used government resources to find Appellant; government unlikely to search nationwide for him.

propositions.text: Appellant could live in Karachi without fear of persecution and it would be reasonable for him to do so.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant could live in Karachi without fear that the agents of persecution would find him in that city. The RAD further finds it would be reasonable for the Appellant to live in Karachi.

propositions.text: Appellant is well educated, multilingual, and Karachi is diverse with opportunities for work, residence, and schooling.
propositions.quote: He is a XXXX with both XXXX and XXXX XXXX. He is well educated and speaks Urdu, English and Punjabi. As noted earlier, Karachi is a very large city and has ethnically and religiously diverse communities. The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that the Appellant would either be able to find work or set up his own business in Karachi, that he and his family would be able to find a residence, and his children would be able to attend school.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant could reasonably live in Karachi without fear, with opportunities for work, residence, and schooling.

propositions.text: Karachi is a viable IFA and there is no serious possibility or personal risk of persecution there for the Appellant.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, after considering all of the evidence, and given the Appellant's past and present circumstances, that Karachi is a viable IFA and that there is not a serious possibility that he would suffer persecution in Karachi or on a balance of probabilities a personal risk of harm in Karachi.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes Karachi is a viable IFA with no serious possibility or personal risk of persecution for the Appellant.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is not a refugee or person in need of protection.
